concepts.name: Defining Characteristics: Money Market vs Capital Market
key_dimensions: Maturity threshold: instruments up to 1 year (money market) vs beyond 1 year (capital market) — UPSC trap on borderline instruments
Purpose distinction: liquidity management/working capital vs long-term investment/fixed capital formation
Risk-return profile: low risk-low return (money market) vs higher risk-higher return (capital market)
Participants overlap: commercial banks participate in both — common confusion point

concepts.name: Call Money and Notice Money Market
key_dimensions: Call money: overnight borrowing (1 day); notice money: 2–14 days — precise distinction frequently tested
Participants: scheduled commercial banks and primary dealers ONLY (non-bank entities excluded — UPSC trap)
Role in CRR maintenance and inter-bank liquidity adjustment
Call money rate as a benchmark and its relationship with Repo Rate corridor

concepts.name: Treasury Bills (T-Bills): Structure and Significance
key_dimensions: Variants: 91-day, 182-day, 364-day — issued by Government of India, NOT state governments (common trap)
Issued at discount, redeemed at face value — zero coupon nature
T-Bills as risk-free benchmark instruments and their role in Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF)
Distinction from Cash Management Bills (CMBs): CMBs have maturity less than 91 days — frequently confused

concepts.name: Commercial Paper (CP): Issuance and Eligibility
key_dimensions: Issued by corporates, Primary Dealers, and All-India Financial Institutions — NOT banks (UPSC trap)
Maturity range: minimum 7 days to maximum 1 year
Unsecured instrument — backed only by issuer's creditworthiness; minimum credit rating required
Issued in denominations of ₹5 lakh and multiples — denominations matter for exam

concepts.name: Certificate of Deposit (CD): Features and Issuer Distinction
key_dimensions: Issued by scheduled commercial banks AND select All-India Financial Institutions — NOT NBFCs (trap)
Maturity: banks issue for 7 days to 1 year; FIs issue for 1 year to 3 years — asymmetric maturity is a trap
Negotiable instrument, issued at discount — difference from Fixed Deposit (FD) which is non-negotiable)
Comparison with Commercial Paper: CP by corporates, CD by banks — frequently swapped in options

concepts.name: Repo and Reverse Repo: Money Market Instruments vs Policy Tools
key_dimensions: Repo as a collateralized short-term borrowing instrument — dual role as money market instrument AND monetary policy tool
Repo vs Reverse Repo direction trap: RBI absorbs liquidity via reverse repo (RBI borrows), injects via repo (RBI lends)
LAF corridor: Repo Rate as ceiling, SDF (Standing Deposit Facility) Rate as floor since April 2022 — replaced reverse repo as floor
Market Repo vs RBI Repo distinction — market participants can also do repo among themselves

concepts.name: Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) vs Reverse Repo Rate
key_dimensions: SDF introduced in April 2022 RBI Monetary Policy — replaced reverse repo as the LAF floor rate
Key distinction: SDF absorbs liquidity WITHOUT providing collateral to banks — uncollateralized absorption (trap)
SDF rate currently set 25 bps below Repo Rate; Reverse Repo Rate remains in RBI toolkit but dormant
Significance: removes RBI's need to hold government securities for liquidity absorption — balance sheet implication

concepts.name: Marginal Standing Facility (MSF): Emergency Liquidity Window
key_dimensions: Banks can borrow overnight from RBI at MSF rate (25 bps above Repo Rate) — forms the LAF corridor ceiling
Banks can pledge SLR securities BEYOND the mandatory SLR limit — up to 2% of NDTL (trap: this dips into SLR)
Distinction from Repo: MSF is a standing facility (bank's right to borrow), Repo is at RBI's discretion under LAF
MSF vs Bank Rate: Bank Rate has no collateral requirement; MSF requires government securities as collateral

concepts.name: Primary Market vs Secondary Market in Capital Markets
key_dimensions: Primary market: new securities issued (IPO, FPO, Rights Issue) — company receives funds; secondary market: trading of existing securities
SEBI's regulatory jurisdiction over both, but different mechanisms (ICDR Regulations for primary; trading regulations for secondary)
Price discovery: primary market price set by book building or fixed price; secondary market through continuous auction
Common trap: Stock exchanges (BSE, NSE) are secondary market institutions, but have a platform for primary issuance too (SME IPOs)

concepts.name: Debt Market Instruments: G-Secs, Corporate Bonds, and Debentures
key_dimensions: Government Securities (G-Secs): issued by Central Government; State Development Loans (SDLs) by state governments — distinction matters
Corporate bonds vs debentures: in India, often used interchangeably but debentures are unsecured while bonds are secured — legal nuance
Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs) as a capital market instrument — issued by RBI on behalf of Government, listed on exchanges
RBI as debt manager for G-Secs vs SEBI regulating corporate bonds — regulatory overlap is a trap

concepts.name: SEBI vs RBI: Regulatory Jurisdiction Overlap in Financial Markets
key_dimensions: RBI regulates: money markets, G-Sec market, forex market, banking system
SEBI regulates: equity markets, corporate bond markets, mutual funds, FPIs in capital markets
Hybrid instruments (e.g., CDs, CPs traded in secondary market) — RBI issues guidelines but SEBI has trading oversight
FSDC (Financial Stability and Development Council) as apex body for inter-regulatory coordination — above both RBI and SEBI

concepts.name: Mutual Funds as Bridge Between Money Market and Capital Market
key_dimensions: Liquid Funds and Overnight Funds invest in money market instruments (T-Bills, CPs, CDs, Repos)
Equity Funds and Debt Funds invest in capital market instruments — SEBI regulates all categories
Money Market Mutual Funds (MMMFs): invest exclusively in money market instruments with maturity up to 1 year
NAV-based pricing vs fixed pricing — liquid funds have T+1 NAV applicability (recent SEBI change — trap)

concepts.name: Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) in Indian Capital Markets
key_dimensions: FPI investment limits: 24% of paid-up capital in equity (can be raised to sectoral cap by board resolution)
FPI in G-Secs: subject to Fully Accessible Route (FAR) and General Route limits — RBI-SEBI dual regulation trap
FPI vs FDI distinction: FPI is portfolio investment (less than 10% stake); FDI is 10% or more with management intent
Volatility concern: FPI flows cause 'hot money' problem — sudden reversal impacts exchange rate and capital markets simultaneously

concepts.name: IPO Mechanism: Book Building vs Fixed Price Method
key_dimensions: Book building: price discovered through bidding (QIBs, NIIs, Retail investors) — 75% must be through book building for mainboard
Price band: floor price and cap price (cap cannot exceed 120% of floor — SEBI rule, frequently tested)
Reservation quotas: QIB 50%, Non-Institutional Investors 15%, Retail Individual Investors 35% — exact percentages are UPSC traps
Green Shoe Option (Over-allotment option): allows stabilization of post-listing price — allowed up to 15% of issue size

concepts.name: Yield Curve and Its Macroeconomic Significance
key_dimensions: Normal yield curve: longer maturity = higher yield; inverted yield curve as recession predictor — conceptual trap
G-Sec yield as benchmark for all other interest rates in the economy — transmission mechanism
Yield vs Price inverse relationship: rising yields = falling bond prices — fundamental concept tested in application questions
RBI's Open Market Operations (OMOs) and Operation Twist as tools to manage yield curve shape

concepts.name: NBFC Regulation and Their Role in Capital/Money Markets
key_dimensions: NBFCs regulated by RBI but CANNOT accept demand deposits — key distinction from banks (trap)
NBFCs can issue Commercial Paper and NCDs (Non-Convertible Debentures) to raise funds from capital markets
Scale-Based Regulation (SBR) framework for NBFCs: Base Layer, Middle Layer, Upper Layer, Top Layer — 2021 RBI framework
NBFCs excluded from Call Money market participation but can access Repo market — exclusion is frequently tested

concepts.name: Difference Between Equity and Debt Financing in Capital Markets
key_dimensions: Equity: ownership claim, residual claim on assets, no fixed obligation — dilutes promoter ownership
Debt: creditor claim, fixed interest obligation, priority over equity in liquidation — tax shield on interest
Hybrid instruments: Compulsorily Convertible Debentures (CCDs) treated as FDI, not debt — RBI classification trap
Debt-to-Equity ratio and its implications for capital structure — Modigliani-Miller theorem context for advanced questions

concepts.name: Stock Exchanges: BSE, NSE, and Market Infrastructure
key_dimensions: BSE (est. 1875): oldest stock exchange; SENSEX = 30 stocks; NSE (est. 1992): NIFTY 50 = 50 stocks
SENSEX base year: 1978-79 with base value 100; NIFTY base year: November 3, 1995 with base value 1000 — trap on base values
Clearing corporations: NSE Clearing Ltd., BSE's Indian Clearing Corporation — separate from exchanges (SCC framework)
SME platforms: BSE SME and NSE Emerge for small companies — different listing norms than mainboard

concepts.name: Capital Market Reforms: Key Milestones and Their Significance
key_dimensions: SEBI establishment: 1988 (as non-statutory body) → 1992 (statutory body via SEBI Act) — year trap (1988 vs 1992)
Dematerialization: NSDL (1996) and CDSL (1999) — elimination of physical share certificates; CDSL is listed entity (trap)
T+1 settlement cycle introduced by SEBI from 2023 for equity markets — India among first globally for T+1
ASBA (Application Supported by Blocked Amount): funds blocked, not debited until allotment — mandatory for all IPO applicants since 2016

concepts.name: Inflation-Indexed Bonds and Sovereign Gold Bonds: Special Debt Instruments
key_dimensions: Inflation-Indexed Bonds (IIBs): principal and interest linked to CPI — protects real value; issued by RBI on behalf of Govt.
Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs): denominated in grams of gold; interest 2.5% p.a. on initial investment value; capital gains tax exempt on maturity (8 years) — tax treatment is a trap
SGBs issued by RBI, listed on NSE/BSE — dual classification as money market or capital market (maturity-based: capital market)
Distinction: SGBs substitute physical gold demand; IIBs substitute inflation-hedge demand — policy objectives differ
